segments.translation: Now we’re going to talk in Cherokee for a little while.

segments.translation: So, we’re going to talk about the questions they have written.

segments.text: ᏓᎦᎵᏍᏙᏗᏍᎬᏃ ᎡᎵᏭ ᎫᏍᏗ ᏯᎾᏕᏠᎦ ᏗᎾᏕᎶᏆᏍᎩ ᎠᎢᏂᏬᏂᎲ

segments.text: ᏃᎴ Ꮎ ᏍᏊ huh… huh ᏍᎩᏃ ᏳᏍᏗ ᏞᎦ ᏓᏂᏢᏃᎮᏟ ᎠᏣᎳᎩᎭ

segments.text: ᏍᎩᏭ... ᏍᎩᏭ ᎢᎦ ᏥᏬᏂᏍᎬ ᎠᏩᎴᏅ ᏕᎦᏕᎶᏆᏍᎬ Ꭷ... ᎧᎾᏥᏍᏕᏥ ᎠᏃᏎᎰ Ballou

segments.text: mhmm yeah Ꮩ ᏣᎵᏍᏓᏂᏙᎸ ᎠᎬᏱ ᏣᎴᏅ

segments.text: ᏙᏳ ᏍᏓᏯ ᏥᎨᏒ ᎠᏎᏃ ᏗᏕᏲᎲᏍᎩ Stilwell ᏓᏳᎶᏒ ᎤᎷᏨ 1936

segments.translation: And I was baptized at Ballou Baptist Church back in 1948. I’m still a member there. I’m still a deacon. I was made a deacon there in 1986. I worked as a deacon a lot.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Was Ben Canoe your pastor then?

segments.text: ᎤᏍᏆᏂᎩᏗᏴᏛ ᏂᎦᏛᏁᎸ ᎠᏗᏍᎨ ᎨᎮ ᏥᏈᏍᏗ ᏳᏩᎦᏗ ᎠᏣᏙᎲᏍᎬ and to me like Amazing Grace that’s what it is
segments.translation: “God has done really amazing things for us,” is what he would say a lot when he was preaching. And to me like Amazing Grace, that’s what it is.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᎠᏎᏅ Amazing Grace in ᏲᏁᎦ don’t seem like as powerful as ᎬᏩᎦᏘᏴ ᏁᏣᏛᏁᎸ
segments.translation: But Amazing Grace in English don’t seem like as powerful as he gave us everlasting life.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᏙᏳ ᎠᎨ... ᎠᎨ... ᎠᏎ ᏍᏊ ᎡᏙᏓ ᎧᎾᏥᏍᏎᏕᏥ ᏍᏊ ᏧᏙᏱᏓ ᎨᎲ ᎧᎾᏥᏍᏎᏕᏥ ᎠᏃᏎᎰ and the Baptist Church.
segments.translation: Really. But also my dad’s name was Ballou, and Ballou is also what they call that Baptist Church.

segments.text: Ballou. ᎠᏎ ᏙᏳ ᏙᎦᏙᎥ ᎨᏎ great great grandpa ... ... ... ᎠᏮᎨᏩᏛ
segments.translation: Ballou. But our real name was… Great-great-Grandpa… I really forgot.

segments.text: Yeah. ᎾᎨ ᏣᏛᏏ... huh... Ꮳ... ᏥᏣᏕᏅ ᎾᎨ ᏣᏛᏏᏙᎴ ᎧᎾᏥᏍᏕᏦ ᎾᎥ
segments.translation: Yeah. Were you born there or did you grow up there, close to Ballou Baptist Church?

segments.text: May 24, I’ll soon be 90 next… Next year.
segments.translation: May 24, I’ll soon be 90 next… Next year.

segments.text: ᏙᏳ ᏍᏊ ᎣᏍᏓ physically but I broke my hip ᏑᏓᎵ ᎾᏕᏘᏴᏓ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏥᏙᎦᏭ ᏍᏊ ᎠᏩᎦᏔᎲᏒ... huh ᎠᏩᎦᏔᎲᏒ and ᎠᎩᏒᏙᏍᎬ ᎤᎾ
segments.translation: I’m doing really good too, physically, but I broke my hip six years ago. I was just standing too, and I turned and I went straight down right there.

segments.text: ᎠᎩᎾ Ꮭ ᏯᏩᎾᏔ ᎡᎳ... I use a walkᎢ but huh

segments.translation: Yeah. Well I’ve spoken to one of your brothers I think… Huh what was his name?

segments.translation: Yeah, he came over and we talked.

segments.text: ᎣᏍ... ᏬᏟ ᎣᏏ ᎤᏬᏂᏍᏗ ᏣᎳᎩ ᏍᎩᎾ

segments.translation: I was in the Marine Corps for ten years.

segments.text: ᎮᏍᏗ ᏣᎳᎩ ᎠᎩᏛᎦᏅ ᏱᎨᎮ ᎠᏮᎨᏩᏏᏙᎸ ᎤᏣᏘ
segments.translation: I didn’t hear any Cherokee, I forgot a lot.

segments.translation: Locust Grove, yeah. What was it like when you were growing up there, were there many houses close by?

segments.text: ᎾᎮᎾ ᏧᎾᏕᎶᏆᏍᏗ ᎾᎴ ᏧᏂ... ᏧᏂᎳᏫᏍᏗ ᏥᎩ ᏅᎩ ᎮᎾ ᏦᎢ ᎢᏳᏟᎶᏓ ᏓᏲᏥᏁᎸ
segments.translation: There was just a school, and a church, and we lived about three or four miles away.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Y’all were coming from there, yeah.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.translation: From our house when I started school, I would go three miles.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏍᎩᏰ ᏍᏊ ᎯᎳ ᏄᏴᏞ ᎡᎳ ᎭᎢᏎ
segments.translation: No matter how cold it was you were still walking?

segments.text: ᎤᏴᏞ ᏱᎩ ᎪᎳ ᏱᎩ ᎡᎳᎮᏍᏗ ᎭᎢᏎ
segments.translation: When it was cold in the winter you were still walking?

segments.text: Ꮟ ᏕᎦᏕᎶᏆᏍᎬ ᏴᏓᎭᏲ ᏴᎩᎨᏱᏗᎨᎲ ᏦᏞᏍᏗᏭ ᎭᏩ
segments.translation: Sometimes they wouldn’t let me go. “Stay home!” Ok.

segments.translation: Were you talking English when you started school?

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.translation: No, I didn’t. I also didn’t --

segments.text: ᏣᎳᎩᏴ Ꮭ ᏍᏊ ᏲᏁᎫ hi ᏴᎾᏗ ᎲᏛ ᎪᎵᎦ but ᏙᏳ ᎮᎾ ᏍᏓᏯ ᏚᎶᏫᏍᏓᏁᎸ ᎠᏪᏲᏅ ᏍᎩᎾ Ꮥ... ᏕᏫ ᏗᏕᏲᎲᏍᎩ ᎠᏃᏎᎮ
segments.translation: -- All Cherokee. Also if they just said “Hi” in English, I didn’t understand. But that teacher they called Dave worked really hard to try and teach me English.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes do you think about the times that you were growing up?

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.translation: I always do nowadays, as I get older.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: uh huh yeah Ꮎ ᎮᎾ ᏄᏍᏗᏓᏅ ᏗᏣᏛᏒ ᏍᎩᎮ ᏫᎪᏘᏍᎪ ᎭᏓᎾᏖᏢᏍᎬ
segments.translation: Uh huh yeah. Do you see things the way it was when you think about it?

segments.text: ᎥᎥ ᏙᏳ ᏍᏊ ᎣᏍᏛ ᎡᏙᏗ ᎮᎾ Ꭱ... ᎡᏥ ᏗᏣᎳᏫᏥᏙᎰ ᎨᎮ
segments.translation: It was really good because Dad and Mom went to church back then.

segments.translation: I was taught well growing up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: yeah, ᏙᎨ ᏧᏙᏱᏓ ᎨᎮ ᏣᏙᏓ ᏃᎴ ᏣᏥ Ꮩ ᏧᎾᏙᏱᏓ

segments.text: …and Ella Mae Butler was her maiden name before she was married to my dad.
segments.translation: …and Ella Mae Butler was her maiden name before she was married to my dad.

segments.translation: Butler. My mom’s dad was ᏥᏗᎩ Butler.

segments.text: Butler mmhm ᎾᏃ ᏣᏙᏓ ᏥᎨᎮ ᎤᏙᏓ Ꮩ ᏚᏙᎡ ᏣᏚᏥ
segments.translation: Butler. And your dad’s dad’s name? Your uncle? [unclear]

segments.text: Tom Ballou Ꮎ ᎤᏛᏏᏙᎵ ᎨᎮ Ꮝ... ᏍᏊ
segments.translation: So, I guess he grew up around there too?

segments.text: ᎥᎥ ᏂᏓᏳᏂᎶᏒ ᎾᎯᏳ ᏃᏭ allotments ᏥᏓᏂᏁᎮ ᏏᏅ ᏓᏂᏁᎮ ᎠᏂᏣᎳᎩ ᎥᎾ ᏭᏂᎷᏨ ... and my great great Grandpa, Jeff Ballou
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s where they came from then. Allotments all the Cherokees had when they arrived… and my great-great-grandpa Jeff Ballou.

segments.text: Jeff Ballou Ꮭ ᏍᏊ ᏙᏳ Ballou ᏦᎦᏙ 1886 I looked in this family tree I got one but I los… I did have someone took it from me I Jeff Foster….
segments.translation: Jeff Ballou. Also, our real name isn’t Ballou. 1886… I looked in this family tree. I got one but someone took it from me. “I, Jeff Foster --

segments.translation: That was y’all’s name at first?

segments.text: ᏙᏳ Ꮩ... Ꮩ... Ꮩ... ᏦᎦᏙ I Jeff Foster na.. change my name to Jeff Ballou 1886 ᏍᎩᎮᎾ ᎠᏁᏟᏔᏅ let’s see ᏏᏛ ᎠᎩᏄᎸᎲᏍᎦ ᎠᏆᏅᏓᏗᏍᏗ but interpretation I can’t get it the break of dawn
segments.translation: -- Our real name. “I, Jeff Foster, change my name to Jeff Ballou. 1886.” The translation, let’s see, I still can’t remember. But the interpretation, I can’t get it: “The break of dawn.”

segments.translation: The wasps come out then at 4:00 am.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: Locust Grove area but I… Marine Corps ᏍᎪᎯ ᏧᏕᏘᏴᏓ ᎠᎩᏴᏢ Marine Corps… and… Korean Conflict I w… I was 19 year old when I was in Korea and ᏃᎴᏅ ᎠᏓᏃ ᏅᏓᎴᏂᏍᎬᏂ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏏᏅ Vietnam ᏔᎵ ᏧᏕᏘᏴᏓ ᏏᏅ ᏅᏓᎴᏂᏍᎬᏂ ᏓᏃ 18 Ꮩ ᎠᏗ ᏣᎳᎩ ᎬᏗ ᏁᎳᏚ
segments.translation: Locust Grove area. But I joined the Marine Corps. I was in the Marine Corps for ten years and Korean conflict. I was 19 years old when I was in Korea, and two years before the Vietnam War started. How do you say 18 in Cherokee, 18?

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᏁᎳᏚ ᏲᏥ ᏚᏑᏰᏒ only Pentagon knew ᎪᏪᎵ ᎪᏪᎶᏗ back home ᏞᏍᏗ ᎤᎾᏛᏅ ᏞᏍᏗ ᎪᏪᎳᏅ ᎪᏪᎵ ᏁᎳᏚᏛ ᏲᏥ ᎣᎦᏑᏰᏒ and 2nd World War ᏥᎨᏒ ᎮᎾ ᏚᏂ.. ᏚᏂᏲᎯᏍᏔᏅ reconnaissance people no more recon but they knew the war was gonna come something like that was gonna happen ᏍᎩ ᎢᏳᏍᏗ ᏃᏭ... ᎠᎬᏱ ᎣᎦ... ᏒᏃᏱ ᏙᎩᎸᏫᏍᏓᏁᎮ ᎢᎦᏅ ᏃᏭ ᎣᏣᎸᏪᏐᎸᏍᏗᎮ ᎣᎦᏓᏐᎸᏍᏙᏗ ᏒᏃᏱ ᎠᏰᏟ ᏙᎩᎸᏫᏍᏓᏁᎮ ᏕᎦᏅᏃ ᏂᎨᏐ ᎣᎦᎴᏅᎲ ᏙᏥᏍᎪᏍᎪ ᎢᏳᏍᏗ like foundation ᏳᏍᏗ then we knew that one day we’d have many trucks traveling on it.
segments.translation: They picked 18 of us and only the Pentagon knew. They said not to write letters back home. They chose 18 of us and the Second World War reconnaissance people. No more recon… but they knew the war was gonna come. Something like that was gonna happen. We’d work at night and rest in the daytime. We used to work late at night. We used to work on the roads digging foundations. We knew that one day we’d have many trucks traveling on it.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᎠᏎᏅ ᎡᎵᏭ ᏂᎦᏓ ᎣᎩᎷᏨ ᎤᏍᏆᏂᎩᏗ ᎣᎩᏪᏎᎸᏃ even the title say that we’re proud ᎩᎶ village ᏲᎩᎷᏨ ᏓᏓᏁᎶ grass huts ᎠᏎᏃ Ꮭ ᎩᎶ ᏰᏙᎥ ᎠᎦᎴᏅ ᎠᎾᏕᎳᎰᏍᎬ ᏱᎪᎩᎪᎰ
segments.translation: But we all came back. It was amazing what they told us, even the title say that we’re proud (The Few. The Proud. The Marines.) When we came to a village building—grass huts—and there wasn’t anybody around… as soon as they seen us they knew something was up.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᎠᎾᏗᏍᎦᏢᏍᎬ ᎣᎪᏩᏛᎲᏃ Ᏻ... ᏢᏳ... Ᏸ... ᎥᎾ ᎠᎾ...ᎠᎾ...ᎠᎾᏗᏍᎦᏢᏍᎬ ᏳᏩᎦᏗᏗᏒᏃ Ꭺ...ᎬᎦᏎᏗᎲ ᎪᏪᎶ Ꮑ... ᏣᏁᎵᏥᏊ ᏳᏟᎶᏓ (unclear) ᎨᏒ ammunition dumps reinforced doors below ground and hospitals ᏍᎩᎾ ᎢᏳᏍᏗ ᎣᎩᏕᎸᎰᏒᏅ and ᏃᏭ ᏗᎣᎦᏂᎩᏒ ᎡᎵᏃ ᏦᎢᏁᏢ ᏅᎩᏁ ᎴᏱᎩ chaplain of the ship says you guy are lucky out of 18 men all of you come home and now we’re gonna take you back to Okinawa ᎾᏃ Okinawa ᏬᎩᎷᏨ Ballou you’re up for re… re-up hm-mm ᎤᏁᎳᏅ ᎮᎾ ᎠᏬᏔᏅ ᏱᎭᏌᎵᏛᏅ ᎮᎾ ᏔᎵᏁ Ꮭ ᏱᏛᎯᎷᏣ ᎠᏬᏎᎸ ᏳᏍᏗᏭ ᏥᎩ ᎠᎩᏛᎦᏅ Ꮭ ᎮᎾ ᏱᎦᎯᎷᎦ Ꮩ ᎭᏗ ᏓᎦᏛᏁᎵ ᏗᏣᎶᏫᏍᏓᏁᏛ ᏥᎨᎮ ᏏᏅ ᏥᎨᎮ ᎯᏄᎪᏣᏭ ᏕᏣᎶᏫᏍᏓᏁᎸᏭ ᏃᏭ ᏬᏟ ᎮᎾ ᎤᎵᎮᎵᏍᏗ ᏙᏳ ᏄᏍᏛᏅ Pryor...ᎫᏩᏲ industrial area and now ᎠᏩᏁᏟᏛᏅ ᏗᎩᎶᏫᏍᏓᏁᏗ and huh Case Tractor ᏓᏃᏢᏍᎬ foundry ᎥᎾ ᎠᏩᎴᏅᎲ ᏓᎩᎶᏫᏍᏓᏁᎲ ᏅᎩᏍᎪ ᏧᏕᏘᏴᏓ ᏓᎩᎶᏫᏍᏓᏁᎸ 15 minutes from home ᏴᏓᎭ ᏳᏍᎦᏃᎵ 17 minutes ᏱᏫᏥᎷᎪ back and forth
segments.translation: We found where they were hiding. And then I started keeping watch, because it was 800 feet down. [Unclear] Ammunition dumps, reinforced doors below ground, and hospitals three stories down. And then when we came back the third or fourth time the chaplain of the ship said “You guys are lucky—out of 18 men all of you came home. Now we’re gonna take you back to Okinawa.” We came back to Okinawa. Then they said “Ballou you’re up for reenlistment.” Hmm, God told me not to go. “If you raise your hand you ain’t coming back,” I heard it clear. “You won’t come back,” He said. I thought: what am I going to do? But He said “You used to work, so get out and just work and work again.” I was happy and relieved. I worked at Pryor Industrial Area. They were making Case Tractors at the foundry when I started working there. I worked there 40 years 15 minutes from home, sometimes it was 17 minutes to go back and forth.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᏦᎢᏁ ᏧᏕᏘᏴᏓ ᎠᏩᎴᏅᏓᏃ ᎢᏓᏁᎸᏛᏅ ᎡᎩ... ᎡᎩᏌᎳᏓᏁᏗ let’s join union for higher pay ᎦᏥᏲᏎᎸ ᎮᎾ ᏦᎢᎭ ᏅᎩ ᎾᎾᏂ and ᏃᏭ Ꮩ... ᎣᏍᏛ ᏙᎦᏢᏃᎮᏢ ᏌᏭᏃ ᎡᎵᏭᏛ ᏔᎵᏏ ᏯᏪᏂ ᏱᏥᎪᏩᏔ ᎩᎶ ᏍᎩᎾ ᏧᎸᏫᏍᏓᏁ union ᏙᏳ ᎤᎷᏨ ᏂᎦᏓ ᎣᎩᏌᎳᏓᏁᎸ
segments.translation: The third year I was there, I tried to get us a raise. “Let’s join the union for higher pay,” I told them. Then about three or four of us talked about it real good, and one said “If I go to Tulsa I’ll bet I can find someone to work with us about the union.” When it did come we all got a raise.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᎣᏍᏛ ᏗᎩᎸᏫᏍᏓ... ᏗᎩ... Ꭳ... Ꭳ... I didn’t... Ꮭ ᎫᏍᏗ ᏱᏥᎦᏔᎮ about coremaker or nothing about foundry
segments.translation: It was a good place to work. I didn’t know anything about a coremaker or nothing about a foundry.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: new ᎦᏬᏂᎯᏍᏗ ᎨᎮ ᏍᏊ foundry work ᏂᎦᏓ ᏧᏓᎴᏅᏛ ᏃᏭᏛ ᏙᎦᏕᎶᏆᎥ ᏑᏓᎵ ᏱᏅᏓ ᏗᎪᎯᏓ ᏏᏅ... ᏏᏅ ᏙᎩ... ᏃᎩᏴᏅᏗ ᎦᏬ... ᏳᏍᏗ ᎦᏬᏂᎯᏍᏗ ᎨᏒ foundry work ᏧᏓᎴᏅᏓ ᏧᏙᏱᏓ ᎦᏬᏂᎯᏍᏗ
segments.translation: Foundry work had new terminology. Everything was different. So we went to school for six months before Simpson called us to talk about things that we needed to know about foundry work. We had to learn different words and terms for our job.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: Yeah, yeah man yeah huh ᎮᏍᏓᎾ ᏯᏛᏅᏗ ᏗᎧᏃᎩᏍᏙᏗ ᏔᏁᏟᏗᏍᏗ ᏱᎩ ᏢᏴ
segments.translation: Yeah. So you never, for instance, ever played any musical instruments?

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᏝᏛᏭ radio ᏍᏊᏛ ᏱᎩ I get too much static ᎠᏎᏅ ᏗᎧᏃᎩᏍᏗ ᏗᎨᎮ ᎧᎾᏥᏍᏕᏥ ᎠᏩᎴᏅᎲ ᏕᏥᏃᎩᏍᎬ ᏗᎧᏃᎩᏓ ᏍᎪᎯ ᎠᏩᏕᏘᏴᏓ ᎨᎮ... ᎦᎳᏅᏓ ᏍᎩᏛ ᏃᏭ ᎦᎳᏅᏓ great great grandpa ᎦᎳᏅᏓ
segments.translation: No, I can’t. Even if it’s a radio I get too much static. But as far as singing, I started singing at Ballou Baptist Church. I was 10 years old… [recalls from earlier] “ᎦᎳᏅᏓ” That’s it, ᎦᎳᏅᏓ. My great-great-grandpa, ᎦᎳᏅᏓ.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: the break of dawn ᏍᎩᏛ ᏙᏳ ᏙᎦᏓᎳ ᎨᎮ ᎦᎳᏅᏓ ᎠᏎ ᎡᏙᏓ ᏥᎨᎮ ᏃᏭ ᎤᏙᏓ ᎧᎾᏥᏍᏕᏥ ᏃᏭ...
segments.translation: The Break of Dawn, that was really our name, ᎦᎳᏅᏓ. But Dad’s dad was Ballou and --

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎯᎢᏃ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᏘᎧᏃᏱᏍᏗ ᏌᏭ ᏳᏩᎦᏓ ᏥᎨᎲ
segments.translation: Were you a Cherokee singer at one time?

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᏏᏛ ᎪᎯᏥᎩ ᏕᏥᏃᎩᏍᎪ ᏙᏓᏩᏍᎬ ᏂᏕᎦᎵᏍᏓᏁᎬ veterans center ᏅᎩᏍᎪ ᎯᏍᎪ ᎠᎴᏱᎩ ᏃᏥ... ᎣᎦ...
segments.translation: I still am to this day. I sing on Sundays at the Veterans Center, there’s about 40 or 50 of us…

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᏙᏥᎳᏫᎪ ᏃᏅ ᎬᎩᏑᏰᏍᎪ amazing grace ᏗᎧᏃᎩᏍᏗ ᏣᎳᎩ ᏂᎦᏓᏛ ᏅᎩ ᏧᏓᏡᎬ ᏕᏥᏃᎩᏍᎪ ᎤᏂᎮᎵᏣᏃᏅ ᎾᏱᎩ hallway ᏃᎴ ᎢᎦᏓ ᎠᏂᎨᏳ ᏂᎨᏐ martin come here I want you to hear… I want to hear that Cherokee singing and ᏙᏳ ᎮᎾ ᏂᎪᎯᎸ ᏕᏥᏃᎩᏍᎪ ᏃᎴ ᏍᏊ Philippine ladies got a boy and two daughters working there where I’m at VA ᏚᏃᏢᏅ ᏙᏛᎦ ᏗᎪᏎᏗ tape ᏚᏃᏢᏅ ᏕᏥᏃᎩᏍᎬ and huh… they sent it to their relatives in Philippines ᏍᎩᏃ ᏫᏛ ᏗᎾᎵᏏᎾᏫᏍᏗᎰ ᎪᎯᏥᎩ ᎬᏬᏎᎲ ᎮᎾ ᏔᎵ ᎶᏢᎾ... two weeks ago ᎡᎵᏊᏃ ᏣᎳᎩ ᎬᏗ ᏓᏂᏃᎩ they learned it off that tape in Philippines ᎬᏬᏎᎸ ᎮᎾ
segments.translation: Yeah we have church there. They pick me to sing Amazing Grace, and I sing all four verses, and then they're all happy. There’ll be people even in the hallway who say “Martin come here. I want to hear the Cherokee singing.” I really do sing all the time. There's a Filipino lady’s got a boy and two daughters working where I'm at, the VA. They made a tape of me singing, and they sent it to their relatives in the Philippines. They’re practicing that over there. And now here, about two weeks ago, they were singing in Cherokee—they learned it off that tape in the Philippines.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It turned out good, didn’t it?

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᏅᎩᏍᎪ... ᎧᎾᏥᏍᏕᏥ ᎮᎾ ᏥᎩ ᏧᎾᏁᏢᏗ ᏚᎾᏓᏡᎬ ᏅᎩᏍᎪ ᎮᎾ ᏧᏕᏘᏴᏓ Ꮣ... ᏓᏪ... every year ᏏᏊ ᎬᎩᏑᏰᏍᎪ song leader
segments.translation: 40… The Christians at Ballou Baptist Church, for the last 40 years, every year, they choose me again as song leader.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.translation: Martin. I’ve held that position for 40 years.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎡᎵᏭᎨ ᏕᎯᏃᎩ amazing grace ᏌᏊ ᏳᎾᏓ... ᏳᎾᏓᏡᎬ
segments.translation: Can you sing one chorus of Amazing Grace?

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᏂᎦᎵᏍᏛᏅᏛ how ever the lord leads ᎤᏁᎳᏅᎯ ᏔᎵᏁ ᏫᎷᎩ ᏦᎢ ᎴᏱᎦ ᏅᎩ ᏳᏛᏅ ᏱᏂᎦᏛᏁ
segments.translation: That can happen. However the Lord leads. If God wants me to sing two or three or four, I can be doing it.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.translation: My voice was starting to falter.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎡᏘᏴ ᏣᏁᎲ ᎠᏂᏣᎳᎩ ᎭᎾᏛᏗᎰᏛᎲ ᏗᏂᏓᏩᏛᎯᏙᎭ ᏥᎨᏒ
segments.translation: So you remember the Cherokees who lived a long time ago? They used to visit one another?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And then they used to say Gadugi.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And somebody would get sick, and they would all be visiting.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏃᎴ ᎩᎶ ᎠᎴ ᏁᎲᎾ ᏱᏄᎵᏍᏔᎾ ᏍᏊ ᏣᏂᏩᏛᎯᏙᎭ ᏏᎨ ᎭᏓᏅᏖᏍᎪ
segments.translation: Or also if someone passed away, they would visit. Do you still think about that?

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᏍᎩᏛ ᏴᏓᎭ Ꭶ...Ꭶ... ᏂᎪᎯᎸ ᏥᎦ... ᏥᎦᏴᎳᎬ ᎮᎾ ᏂᎬᏩᏍᏗ ᏗᏩᎴᏂᏙᎸ
segments.translation: Yeah, sometimes. It seems like I’m getting too old to remember how it used to be.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᏙᏳ ᎤᏖᏗ ᎣᏍᏓᏛ ᎨᎲ ᎦᏗᎰ ᎮᎾ
segments.translation: It was really enjoyable, I always say it was really good.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᏴᏓᎭ ᎮᎾ ᎡᎵᏏ ᏥᎨᏒ on my mother’s side ᎠᏂᎷᎪ ᎡᏙᏓ ᎮᎾ Ꮵ... ᏂᎪᎯᎸ ᎮᎾ we lived out away from... out on the farm, it wasn’t a big farm but we... ᎠᏎᏅ ᏂᎪᎯᎸ ᎮᎾ ᏓᏂᏍᏓᏲᎯᎲ ᏃᏭ ᎤᏟᎶᏢ ᏃᏭ ᏏᏆ ᎠᎯᎰ ᏃᎴᏅ thanksgiving ᎾᎴᏱᎩ ᎾᎯᏳ ᏃᏭ ᏭᏟ ᎣᏍᏓ ᎨᎲ ᏚᎾᏓᏩᏛᎯᏙ ᎣᏍᏗ... ᎠᏁᏙᎰ ᏴᏓᎭ ᏒᎾᏙᏓᏩᏍᏗ ᏱᎪᎯᏓ ᏃᏭ ᏯᎾᏂᎩ
segments.translation: And sometimes my grandma, on my mother’s side, would come over. And my dad… always… We lived away, out on a farm. Wasn’t a big farm, but around Christmas we were always killing a pig. Or if it was Thanksgiving. It was really good to visit each other then. They would stay for about a week and then go home.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: yeah, ᎾᎨ ᎢᎾᎨ ᏳᏕᏅ ᎫᏍᏗ ᏍᎩᏛᎮ ᏍᏊ ᎢᏣᎵᏍᏓᏴᎲᏍᎬ ᎢᏥᎲᎸ ᎢᏥᎩᏍᎨ
segments.translation: Did you all eat stuff that came from the wild, is that what y’all looked for too?

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᏌᎶᎵᏛ ᏥᏍᏚᏅ ᎫᏇᏅ ᏍᎩᎮᎾ ᎾᏬᏎᎮ ᎡᏙᏓ ...just when I was growing, able enough to eat ᏪᎮ ᏓᎬᏲᏎᎲ ᏌᏊ ᏔᎵ ᎴᏱᎩ ᏍᏊ ᎾᎩᏤᎰ ᏃᎴᏅ ᎣᏍᏓ ᏂᎬᏁᎰ ᏬᏱ ᎮᎾ ᏂᎩᏍᎬ ᎭᏫᏯ ᏣᏛᏒ ᎠᏬᏞᎮ ᎨᎰ ᎠᏎᏅ ᏌᎶᎵ ᏥᏍᏚᏅ ᏂᎨᏐ ᎾᎯᏳ ᎮᎾ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏍᏊ ᎠᏫ ᏥᎩ ᎨᏍᏗ ᏯᏁᎮ ᏙᏳ ᎤᏓᏅᎯᏓ since about 1950 before I ever saw the deer around that community.
segments.translation: Squirrels, rabbits, and quails. That’s what my dad used to tell me… Just when I was grown, ‘able enough to eat. I went and looked for one or two quail, and that's all I could bear. He would fix them for me and that meat is what I was raised on. And also squirrels and rabbits back then. As for deer, there wasn’t any for a really long time. About 1950 before I ever saw a deer around that community.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: ‘Wonder what the reason for that was?

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᎩᎳᏛ ᏚᎾᏘᏃᏢ ᎢᎾᎨ ᏓᏂᏲᏏᏙᎲ ᎪᎯᏥᎩ ᏙᏳ ᎠᎦᏎᏍᏙᏗ ᏅᏃ
segments.translation: They brought them recently and let them go in the woods. Nowadays you really have to watch out for them on the road.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᎤᏂᎪ... ᎤᏂᎪᏓᏛ ᎠᏁᎯ ᎪᎯᏥᎩ ᎠᏫ ᏂᎬᏛ ᏍᏊ
segments.translation: There’s a lot of deer nowadays, everywhere too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏂᎬᏛ yeah Ꮎ ᏥᏣᏛᏏᏗᏒ ᎢᎾᎨ ᎡᎯ ᏯᏛᏂ ᏒᎩ ᎫᏩᏯ ᎠᎴᏱᎩ ᏃᎴ ᏜᎢᏓ ᏱᎩ ᏃᎴ ᎠᏥᎳ ᏱᎩ ᎠᎹᏱ ᎦᏄᎪᎪ ᎤᏕᏅ ᏍᎩᎨ ᎢᏳᏍᏗ
segments.translation: Yeah, everywhere. When you were growing up would you say wild onion? Or how about huckleberry or poke or watercress by a spring, or something like that?

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.translation: Watercress. I know all about that growing up.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.translation: I like mushrooms the best. What they called wishi.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It was really good to eat.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: man yeah ᏎᏃ ᎪᎯᏴᏥᎩ Ꮭ ᎰᏩ ᏍᎩ ᎢᏳᏍᏗ ᎠᏂᎩᏍᏗ ᏙᎭ
segments.translation: Man, yeah. But nowadays they don’t really eat that kind of stuff, huh?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏃᏭ ᏗᏂᏲᏟ ᎢᏯᏛᎾᏗ ᏗᎦᏳᎾᏚᎵ ᏗᏂᏲᏟ ᏍᎩ ᎢᏳᏍᏗ ᎤᏂᎩᏍᏗ
segments.translation: But nowadays children wouldn’t really want to eat that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess your parents taught you a lot of things.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᎡᏙ... ᎤᏙ... ᏭᎪᏗᏕ ᏍᎩ ᎢᎾᎨ ᎡᎯ ᎠᎵᏍᏕᎵᏙᏗ ᎨᎲ ᎠᎴ ᏍᏊ ᎾᎮᎾ ᎧᎾᏥᏍᏕᏥ ᎠᏃᏎᎰ ᏧᎾᏕᎶᏆᏍᏗ ᎢᎾ ᎮᎾ ᏓᏲᎦᎴᏅᎲ ᎠᏫᏒᏅ ᏗᎦᎸ... ᏗᎦᎸᏫᏍᏓᏏ ᎠᎴ ᏍᏊ keeping ᎠᎴ ᎠᎵᏍᏓᏴᏗ ᏕᎨᏒ ᎠᎵᏍᏓᏴᏗ ᏕᎨᎲ had to learn to wash dishes and just do all the kitchen work ᎣᎨᏲᎲᏍᎬ
segments.translation: Yeah, a lot. Like how to use the wild to help yourself. And also—at that Ballou school—we started planting a garden. For work, and also keeping… how the kitchen was. ‘Had to learn to wash dishes and just do all the kitchen work. They were teaching us.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᏃᎴ ᏠᎨᏏ ᎣᏫᏒ ᏕᎨᎲ ᏃᎴ ᎣᎨᏲᎲᏍᎬ Ꮎ ᏕᏫ ᏗᏕᏲᎲᏍᎩ
segments.translation: The teacher, Dave, was teaching us to plant in the field.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: How to make… how to make a garden.
segments.translation: How to make… how to make a garden.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you all make a big place to garden?

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᏣᏁᎳ... about 8... about 8 acres ᏣᏁᎳ ᏳᏟ... Ꮩ ᎭᏗ ᎮᏍᏗ ᏯᏩᎾᏔ Ꮳ... Ꮳ... 8 acres Martin: About eight acres. What would you say? I don’t know… eight acres…

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.translation: Eight acres, could I say that?

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᏚᏯᏭ Ꮎ ᏕᎨᎰ green beans ᏃᎴ Ꮪ.. ᏗᎦᏛᏍᏗ ᏳᏟᎶᏢ Ꮕ ᏥᏃᎮᎲ ᎠᎬᏱ ᏗᎦᎶᎯᏍᏙᏗ ᎨᎲ ᏗᏣᏍᏕᎸᏗ ᎾᎯᏳ Thursday ᎢᏥᎷᎨᏍᏗ ᏗᏥᎦᎸᎵᎨ ᎠᏂᎷᎪ ᎠᏂ... ᎠᏂᎵᏛᏅᏍᎪ ᏳᏍᏙ ᎨᎲ ᏃᎴᏅ
segments.translation: Mostly green beans. We would all come together, like we were talking about earlier—about working and helping each other. They’d tell us “Tell your parents to come on Thursdays too.” We canned everything.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: yeah ᏎᎷ ᏂᎨᎰ ᏄᏂᏅ ᎥᎥ ᏂᎦᏓᏛ ᎠᏫᏒᏗ ᎨᎲ
segments.translation: Yeah, always corn and potatoes. Yeah, we planted everything back then.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᎣᏥᏫᏒᏍᎬ ᏃᎴ working the garden ᎣᎨᏲᎲᏍᎬ ᏱᎬᎾᏗ ᏕᎨᎲ ᎦᎶᎪᏗ ᏚᏓᎴᏒ ᏚᏕᏲᏒ ᏕᏫ ᏗᏕᏲᎲᏍᎩ
segments.translation: We all were planting and working the garden. He was teaching us how to hoe. Dave was teaching different ways.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He really taught you all good.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᎣᏍᏓᏛ ᎣᎨᏲᏅ ᏃᎴ ᏍᎩ ᏍᏊ ᏕᏫ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎩᎶ ᏳᏓᏂᎸ ᎠᏎᏛ ᏕᏫ Ꮲ ᏓᏘᏁᎪ ᎧᏩᏲ ᏱᎩ hospital ᎩᎶ ᏳᏓᏂᎸ ᎤᎪᏗ ᏍᎩᏚ ᏙᎯᏳ ᏥᎨᏳᎢ ᎨᏒ ᏕᏫ
segments.translation: He taught us really good. And even when somebody got sick, Dave he would take them to the hospital in Pryor. If somebody was really sick. I really loved Dave.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏙᏅ ᎠᎩᏟ ᎨᎮ ᏙᎭ ᏍᎩᎾ ᏍᏓᏯ ᏧᎶᏫᏍᏓᏁ
segments.translation: He really worked hard, huh? He worked hard.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᏍᏓᏯᏛ ᏧᎶᏫᏍᏓᏁᎸ ᏁᎲᏁ ᏥᏄᎵᏍᏔᏅ ᏃᎴ ᎠᏯ ᎠᎩᏑᏰᏗ ᎥᎨᏒ ᎦᏬᏂᎯᏍᏗ ᏂᏣᏎᎮ ᎢᎦ ᎯᏬᏂᏒ ᏣᎳᎩ ᎠᏗᏍᎬ ᎤᏬᏪᎸ speak much cherokee as you can as possible Martin when you speak at my funeral ᏙᎯᏳᏛ boy ᏍᏓᏱ ᎨᎲ ᏯᏛᎾᏗ ᎢᎦ ᏥᎨᏳ ᎨᎲ ᎦᏥᎨᏳᏛ ᏴᏫ ᏚᏂᎶᏒ ᎤᎪᏗ ᎨᎲ ᏗᎦᎸᏫᏍᏙᏗ ᏓᎩᎸᏫᏍᏓᏁᎸ ᎦᏗᏍᎪ ᎮᎾ my first love was chainsaw I cut about thousand 2 or 3 thousand about I don’t know how many ricks of wood I cut ᎠᏂᎦᏴᎵ ᏕᎦᏛᏁᎲ truck load I drive.. I drive in the driveway ᎠᏓ ᏕᎬᏯᏃᎯᏏ ᏃᎴ ᏫᏗᏣᏚᎦᏭ ᎦᏳᎳ ᏍᏓᏱ ᏕᏣᎸᏫᏍᏓᏏ ᎬᏬᏎᎰ ᎢᎦᏓ ᎢᎦᏗ ᎠᎭᏂᏛ ᏱᏣᏒᏛᏅ ᎭᏩ ᏃᎴ ᏱᎦᏒᏛᏍᎪ keeping it dry for them ᎤᎪᏗᏛ ᏗᎦᎸᏫᏍᏓᎾᏗ ᎠᎩᎸᏫᏍᏓᏁᎸ
segments.translation: Yeah he was a hard worker, and when he passed away he chose me to be the speaker. “Do all that you can. Speak as much Cherokee as you can, when you speak at my funeral.” It was really hard to do because I really loved him. I loved a lot of people and I worked hard at a lot of different things. Like I said, my first love was a chainsaw. I cut about two or three thousand, about... I don’t know how many ricks of wood I cut. I did it for a lot of older people, truck load I’d drive.. I drive in the driveway. I’d tell em “I brought you some wood.” Some would say “Just throw em out, you already worked real hard.” Some would say “Stack it over here” keeping it dry for them. I worked really hard.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.translation: Sometimes. Sometimes they would just say “Thank you,” and I appreciated that as well.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᎢᎦᏓ ᏃᎴ ᎠᏪᏅᏒ ᎠᏂᎷᎪ ᎦᎴᎼᏛ ᏛᎵᏏ ᎴᏱᎩ ᎠᏧᏣ ᎠᏩᏓᏂᎶᎯᏎ Ꮭ ᎠᏕᎳ ᏯᎩ ᏯᎩ ᎢᎾ ᎠᏪᏓᏍᏙᏗ ᎬᏬᏎᎰ ᏳᏍᏛᏩᏛ ᏥᎩ ᏓᎩᎸᏫᏍᏓᏁᎸ I rolled over in my bed several times several people just took out a $100 bill and give it to them ᏍᎩᏛ ᎾᏩᏍᏗ ᏗᎩᎶᏫᏍᏗ ᏍᎩ ᎮᎾ ᏳᏍᏗ ᎤᏁᎳᏅ ᎠᏩᎵᏍᎪᎵᏍᏓᏁᎲ Ꮟ ᏓᏭᎦᏔ ᎣᏍᏓ ᏗᎦᏓᏁᏗ ᎨᎲ ᏴᏫ
segments.translation: Some would come to my house, in Claremore or Tulsa. “My son is getting sick,” they would say, and “I don’t have the money to travel.” I rolled over in my bed several times several people, just took out a $100 bill and give it to them. That’s the way I am. That’s how God has provided for me, and I still plan on doing the best I can for people. can for people.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎣᏍᏓᏛ ᏣᏓ... ᏣᏓᎾᏙ ᏙᎭ ᏍᎩ ᏱᏄᏍᏛ
segments.translation: So you felt really good huh, when it’s like that?

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᎥᎥ ᎣᏍᏓᏛ ᎥᏪᏲᏅ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎡᏙᏓ ᎮᎾ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏔᎵᏍᎪ ᏧᏕᏘᏴᏓ ᏚᎦᏘᏛ ᎧᎾᏥᏍᏕᏥ one.. from the day appointed... he didn’t go over one... straight 20 years consecutively I know when the Lord called him 80 ᎠᏩᎾᏙ ᎮᎾ ᎠᎬᏱ ᎣᎩᎦᏘᏯ ᏄᏍᏛᏅ ᏅᎩ ᏑᏓᎵᏭ ᎴᏱᎩ ᏃᏥᎥ prayer meeting they kept picking up ᏃᏅ ᏑᏓᎵ ᎦᎵᏉᎩ ᏧᏕᏘᏴᏓ ᏃᏭ ᏔᎵᏍᎪ ᏦᏍᎪ ᏃᏥᎣ ᏃᏅ ᏁᎲᏅ ᏥᏄᎵᏍᏔᏅ ᏁᎳᏍᎪ ᏴᏓᎭ ᏍᎪᎯᏥᏉ ᏃᏥᎣ ᏦᏍᏓ ᏙᎩᏘᏂᏙᎸ ᎠᏯ ᏥᎩ ᎠᏯᏙᎯ ᎨᎲ ᏍᏊ ᎾᎯᏳ ordained.. ordained deacon in church in 86 ᏙᏳ ᎮᎾ ᎾᏅ ᏗᏩᏓᏬᏍᏗ ᎨᎲ ᏣᎾᏓᏍᏕᎵᏍᎬ ᎠᏂᏯᏙᎯ ᎠᎴ ᏗᎦᏘᏯ ᏗᏓᏬᏍᏙᏗ ᏍᎩ ᏗᎩᎸᏫᏍᏓᏁᎸ ᏦᎢᏥᏉ ᏍᎪᎯ ᏱᎨᏎ ᎦᏥᏍᏕᎸᏗ William Bright Ben Canoe Fred Albert my dad and... ᎠᎩᏄᎸᎲᏍᎦᏛ ᎯᏍᎩᏁ
segments.translation: Yeah. I was really taught well because my dad pastored at Ballou Baptist Church for 20 years. From the day appointed… he didn’t go over one… straight 20 years consecutively. I know when the Lord called him. In ‘80. I remember when he first became our pastor there was four or six of us in a prayer meeting. They kept picking up and after six or seven years then there was like 20 or 30 of us. And then, when he passed away, sometimes there would be 80 or 100 of us. He led us really good. As for me, I was a deacon then... Ordained deacon in the church in ‘86. I really helped the other deacons and pastor baptize cause that was part of my job. I helped with 310 baptisms—William Bright, Ben Canoe, Fred Albert, my dad, and I can’t remember the fifth.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So Fred came for a while too huh?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So Fred came for a while too, huh?

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.translation: For about three years, Dennis... No, Littledave.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: Kenneth Littledave me and him we baptized at one time 23 boys and girls ᏌᏭ.. ᎤᏴᏟ ᏍᏊ ᎨᎲ Kenneth Littledave ᎠᎩᎦᏘᏯ
segments.translation: Yeah Kenneth Littledave. Me and him, we baptized 23 boys and girls at one time, and it was cold.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᏙᎯᏳᏛ ᏍᎦᏍᏗᏛ ᎨᎲ hey ᎦᏥᏲᎮᎸ ᏥᏲᎮᎸ ᏌᏭ ᎤᏩᎦᏓ Kenneth ᏝᏍ ᏣᏩᏛᏗ ᏱᎩ ᎪᏪᎸ ᏗᏂᏲᏝ ᎨᏒ Ꮩ ᎤᏍᏗ ᎤᎾᏚᎵᎲ ᎤᏅᏗ ᏥᏲᎮᎸ ᎮᎾ ᏍᏓᏱ ᎮᎾ ᎠᎵᏣᏙᎲᏍᎦ ᏗᏂᏲᏝ ᏥᎩ ᎤᏅᏓᏭ ᎮᎾ ᎢᎦ ᎤᎾᏗᏔᏍᏗ Ꮎ ᎮᎾ that solid food is too powerful Kenneth ᏙᎯᏳ ᎮᎾ ᎤᏓᏅᎯᏓ ᏗᎩᎶᏒ as Christians ᏴᏓᎭ ᏍᏊ ᎠᎴ ᎠᏯ ᎠᏩᏝᏂᎩᏗ ᎮᎾ ᎠᎴ ᎠᏯ ᎠᎩᏄᎸᎲᏍᎪ ᎠᎩᎩᎯᏍᏗ ᏄᏍᏛ ᏕᎭᏕᏲᎲᏍᎬ ᏥᏲᎮᎸ but he was a good minister Kenneth Littledave.
segments.translation: He was real outstanding. And one time I told him “Have you ever found where it says what the children need?” “Milk,” I told him. I told him “You’re preaching too hard, the children just need milk, solid food is too powerful.” “I’ve come a long ways as a Christian,” but sometimes it was even too hard for me to swallow “…what you’re teaching.” But he was a good minister, Kenneth Littledave.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: boy he could play a piano ᏗᎧᏃᎩᏍᏗ ᏥᎨᎲ
segments.translation: Boy, he could play a piano.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When Kenneth decided to, he was funny.

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᏴᏓᎭ ᎮᎾ ᏱᏗᎧᏃᎩᏍᏗ come on Jerry Lee ᏥᏲᎮᎰᏛ ᎯᎢᏛ ᏂᏗᎬᏁᎰ ᏙᎯᏳ ᏂᎦᏓᏲ ᎣᎩᏰᏥᎪ
segments.translation: Sometimes he’d be singing and I’d say “Come on Jerry Lee!” He would do like that, and we would all laugh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He would do just like that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏗᏣᎦᏴᎵᎨ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏃᎴ ᏣᎵᏏ ᏥᎨᎲ Ꮭ ᎫᏍᏗ ᎤᏂᏃᎮᏢ ᏱᎨᎮ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᎤᏪᏘ ᏓᏳᎾᏂᎩᏒ ᎤᎾᏛᎦᏅᎴ ᏱᎨᎮ
segments.translation: Your parents or grandparents never talked or heard anything about when they left North Carolina?

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: ᎠᏎᏃ ᏙᏳ ᎨᏒ ᎠᎴ my mom and dad I love all the people Martin who’s your favorite ᎣᏥᏯᎥ ᏧᏂᎳᏫᏍᏗ who’s your favorite John Wayne ᎠᎾᏗᎰ ᎢᎦᏓ ah no no Martin that was Kenneth Littledave ᎣᎦᏛᏛᏁᎮ Martin who was your favorite? Favorite. Sally Murphy Ballou ᏥᏥᏲᎮᎸ ᎡᎵᏏ boy my Grandma that was the best woman I loved ᏙᏳ ᎮᎾ ᏍᏊ ᎠᏂᏲᏍᎩ ᏃᏭ ᏣᏩᏖᎳᏛ ᎠᎩᏩᏛᎯᏙᎸ ᏏᎾ ᎠᏩᏂᎩᏓ I’ll take you to the same place where I hugged her and she.. ᎠᏎᏛ ᎠᏩᏂᎩᏍᏗ ᏥᏲᎮᎸ ᏝᏛ ᏃᏭ ᎭᎸᎯᏳ ᏔᎵᏁ ᏱᏂᏛᎬᎾᏓᎪᏩᏗ ᎠᏬᏎᎸ ᎮᎾ ᎤᏲᎢᏛ ᏂᏪᏢᏍᎦ.. ᏅᎩ.. 14 months ᎤᏛ ᏛᎦᏁᎸᏗ ᏥᏲᎮᎸ ᎠᏎ ᎾᎯᏳ ᏙᎾᏓᎪᎲᎢ one week ᎠᎩᎷᎸ 14th week ᏓᏩᏂᎩᏍᏗ they sent a telegram in Japan that she was very sick and they told me I could go ahead ᎮᎵᏭᏛ ᏯᎭᏂᎩᏓ we’ll put you on the plane to get you there but ᎠᏎᏅ ᏍᎩ ᏱᎾᏣᏛᏁᎳ you got to make up 14 months ᏒᎾᏙᏓᏩᏍᎦᏭ ᎮᎾ ᏣᎷᎳ by the time you get there and back it’ll been.. it takes 2 to 3 months fly back over here it’ll be another 2 or 3 weeks before you can go and rotate back and put your 14 months in here ᏙᎲ ᏔᏛᏁᎵ I'll just stay and remember her as she was when I left her ᎠᏩᏛᏅ ᎮᎾ ᏙᏳ ᎮᎾ I didn’t make her funeral ᎠᏎᏅ ᎤᏁᎳᏅᎯᏛ ᏫᎯᎷᏨ ᎠᏬᏎᎸ ᎮᎾ ᏫᎯᎷᏨ ᏗᎬᎦᏘᏰᏍᏗ ᎮᏂ ᏗᎧᎸᎬ ᏗᏟ ᎦᎶᎯᏍᏗ ᎢᎾ ᏗᎬᎦᏘᏰᏍᏗ ᏣᏬᏎᎸ ᎮᎾ I’ll meet you at the Eastern gate she told me that ohh it hurt me ᎠᏎᏃ ᏍᎩᎾ ᏥᎦᏘᏲ ᎢᎸᎯᏳ when the Lord calls me ᏦᎢ ᎮᎾ ᎤᏩᎦᏗ ᏗᎩᏐᏨ Ꮎ Pacific I spent over 4 years overseas duty Japan Okinawa Phillipines Korea and Vietnam and Bangkok, Thailand ᏍᎩ ᏍᏊ ᏥᎩ ᎠᎩᏍᏆᏂᎪᏍᎪ ᏚᏂᏲᎱᏎᎴ ᎮᏂ my discharge papers in St. Louis the part where they keep the records can’t prove that I was in North Carolina ᏍᎩ ᏃᏭ ᎠᎹ ᎣᎦᏗᏔᎲ ᎪᎯᏴᏥᎩ ᎯᏍᎩ ᏯᎦᏴᎵ ᎨᎬᏈᏴᎡᎰ the people that were stationed in North Carolina Camp Lejeune ᏞᏍᏗ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᎬᎬᏍᏕᎸᏗ ᏱᎩ ᎠᏯᏅ ᎠᎩᏄᎸᎲᏍᎪ ᎦᏁᏟᏗ we don’t.. we can’t find the record where you were stationed in Camp Lejeune Thailand Bangkok ᏃᎴ Ꮭ ᏍᏊ ᏚᏂᏲᎱᏎᎸ ᏚᎪᏁᎮ ᏗᎪᏪᎵ ᏦᎢ ᏯᎦᏴᎵ ᎮᎾ ᎦᏈᏱᏍᎪ ᏏᏅᏓ ᎤᎾ ᏧᏥᏯ veteran hospital see I draw $4,000 a month on social security and huh ᏲᏁᎦᎭ ᏓᏥᏬᏂᏏ ᏍᏘ ᎠᏩᏍᎦᏎᏗ ᎠᎩᏄᎸᎲᏍᎬ I can’t interpret it back in Cherokee I paid $3,000 a month to stay in Claremore Veteran’s Center I'll be in there 6 years in Janua... February February ᏑᏓᎵ ᏧᏕᏘᏴᏓ that’s over 80,000 bucks boy and huh ᏅᎩᏍᎪ.. Like $4,000 a month I draw and they get $3,000 out of it leaves me $1,000 for my cigarettes and whatever I wanna buy ᏍᎩ ᎫᏍᏗ
segments.translation: But really, my mom and my dad would ask… I love all the people. “Martin who’s your favorite, people in church, who’s your favorite?” Some would say “John Wayne.” Ah no, no, Martin that was Kenneth Littledave: “Martin who was your favorite?” Favorite? Sally Murphy Ballou. Boy, my grandma was the best woman I loved. She came to visit me before I went to the military. I’ll take you to the same place I hugged her. I told her “Well I’ll have to go,” but she said “We’ll never see each other again.” It’s bad for you to say that. I had been away for fourteen months. And the last week of the fourteenth month I got a telegram in Japan saying she was very sick. They said I could leave, “We’ll put you on the plane to get you there” but “you got to make up the fourteen months. By the time you get there and back…” “It takes two to three months to fly back over here. It’ll be another two or three weeks before you can go and rotate back and put your fourteen months in.” So I said I would stay and remember her how she was when I left her. I didn’t make her funeral. She said “If you make it to heaven I’ll be waiting for you, I’ll wait for you at the eastern gate. I’ll meet you at the eastern gate,” she told me that, oh it hurt me. Oh Lord help me, that’s what I wait for when the Lord calls me. I've crossed the Pacific three times. I spent over four years on overseas duty—Japan, Okinawa, the Philippines, Korea, Vietnam, and Bangkok, Thailand. Even that sometimes I don’t understand. They lost my discharge papers. In St. Louis—the part where they keep the records can’t prove that I was in North Carolina. But those people who were in North Carolina, they paid them five thousand dollars for being stationed there. They said “We can’t find the record where you were stationed in Camp Lejeune—Thailand, Bangkok.” They lost those papers. I pay three thousand a month at the veterans hospital. I draw four thousand dollars a month on social security. I'm going to speak a lot in English now ‘cause I'm getting pretty mad. I can’t interpret it back in Cherokee. I pay three thousand a month to stay in Claremore Veteran’s Center, I've been there six years in February. That’s over 80,000 bucks, boy. Like four thousand dollars a month I draw and they get three thousand dollars out of it, leaves me a thousand dollars for my cigarettes and whatever I want to buy.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏥᏣᎴᏅᎲ ᏕᎭᏕᎶᏆᏍᎬ ᏣᏗᎲ ᎪᎯ ᎩᎶᏅ ᏣᎧᎮ ᏣᎵᏍᏕᎵᏍᎩ ᏙᎭ David ᏧᏙᏱᏗ ᏃᏭ ᏲᏁᎦ ᎦᏬᏂᏍᎩ
segments.translation: ‘While ago when you said you started school, you said you had somebody named David, that spoke English.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Could you read Cherokee when you used to go to that church?

segments.speaker: martin-ballou
segments.text: huh uh ᏣᏁᎵ Ꮲ ᏯᏩᏕᏘᏴᏗ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎣᏏ ᏥᏓᏩᏕᎶᏆᎥ ᏂᎪᎸ ᎮᏂ Sunday School ᏙᏣᏕᎶᏆᏍᎬ Ꮎ alphabet A E I O U ᏍᎩ ᏂᎦᏗ ᎠᏩᏕᎶᏆᎥ ᏃᎴ ᎡᎵᏭ ᏃᏭ ᎬᎩᎪᎵᏰᏗ ᎨᎲ ᏃᏭᏅ ᎣᏏ ᎨᏎ ᏍᏊ until I enlisted in the Marine Corps ᏃᏭᏅ ᏓᏩᎨᏩᏐᏅ
segments.translation: No, I was eight years old when I learned at Sunday school. I learned the alphabet, a-e-i-o-u. I learned all of that and I was able to read. And it was ok, and then I enlisted in the Marine Corps and then I forgot all about them.

segments.text: ᎤᎪᏗ ᏦᏚᎯ ᏃᏭ ᏛᏛᏂᏛᎮ ᎨᎵᎲ ᎾᏛ ᎠᏪᏙᎸ ᎧᎾᏥᏍᏕᏦ Ꮎ ᏍᏊ..
segments.translation: I thought you were going to say you’re prettier now. Yeah, I've been there before, Ballou Church.

segments.text: ᎾᎨ Ꮟ ᏅᏯᎭ ᏣᏓᏁᎵᏴ ᎠᏎ ᏧᏂᏲᏍᏛᏅ ᏂᎦᏓ ᎠᏎᏃ ᏣᎨᎦᏁᏍᎨᎮᎸ ᏍᎩ ᏳᏍᏗ ᏙᎦᏛᏂᎸᏨ
segments.translation: Was it back then when that building was all rock? They’ve torn it down and had a new one built, they granted us that.

segments.text: ᎦᏅᏓᏗᎰ Hart ᏧᏙᏱᏗ ᏧᏂᏂᏌᏅ ᏍᏈᏍᏗ ᏙᏒ ᏥᏄᏅᏍᏛᏅ

segments.text: ᏙᏳᏛ ᏌᏭ ᎮᏂ Lester Smith ᏧᏙᏱᏗ ᎠᏩᎴᏅᎲ ᎮᏂ ᏕᎦᏎᎮᎲ each everyone that went and viewed the body ᎠᏗᎲᏅ 2300 ᏏᏅ ᎡᎵᏭ ᏅᎩᏍᎪ ᎯᏍᎪ.. maybe ᏑᏓᎵᏍᎪ ᎴᏱᎩ ᎾᏂᏴ Ꮟ I bet there was 4,000 people there he said I quit at 3600 Gene Leroy Hart ᎠᎩᏍᏓᏴᎲᏍᎩ ᎮᏂ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎠᎬᏱ they were first cousins
segments.translation: Yeah there was, there was one named Lester Smith. When it began I counted each and every one that went and viewed the body—two thousand, three hundred... forty, fifty or sixty… I bet there was 4000 people there. segments.text: ᏍᎩᏛ ᎦᏓᏅᏖᏍᎪ Cedar Tree like.. like year.. ᏑᏕᏘᏴᏗ ᏂᏕᎦᎵᏍᏘᏁᎦ ᏗᎵᏍᏗ ᏣᏃᏎᎰ Jim Chair ᏧᏄᎸᎲᏍᎦ ᏗᎦᏍᎩᎶ oh I remember him
segments.translation: That’s what I think about at Cedar Tree every year. Dilsdi they call him, Jim Chair Tsunulvhsgi Digasgiloi! Oh, I remember him…

segments.text: Bert Spade What about that little feller Dave... ᏙᏳ ᎤᏍᏗ ᎮᏂ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎠᏍᎦᏯ ᏍᎦᏍᏗᏛ ᎮᏂ ᏂᎦᏪᎰ ᎮᏂ ᎠᏬᏎᎲ but I forget who it was ᏦᏣᏁᎶᏂᏙ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏑᏓᎵ ᎦᎵᏉᎩ Ꮲ ᏲᎦᏕᏘᏴᏗ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏁᎵ ᏍᎪᎯ ᏣᏁᎵ maybe 10 year old ᎤᎾᏛ ᎠᎩᎸᏍᎪ ᎤᏂᎵᎬ ᎣᎦᎵᏥᏙᏁᎰ ᎠᏗᎲ I can’t call his name ᏳᏓᎭ ᎢᎦ ᏓᏅᏖᏍᎪ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎠᎩᏄᎸᎲᏍᎪ ᎠᏩᎾᏔᏗᏍᏗ ᏚᏙᎥ
segments.translation: Bert Spade. What about that little feller Dave? He was a really little man. I was told he used to really be a talker, but I forgot who it was. We used to play around when we were about six or seven years old. Eight or maybe ten years old. He would get up there on that stump and preach to us. I can’t recall his name sometimes. I think about that, but I can’t remember his name.
